body_text: View all news CNO Financial Group Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results 07/30/2026 Download (opens in new window) PDF 173 KB CARMEL, Ind. , July 30, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CNO Financial Group, Inc. (NYSE: CNO) today reported its second quarter 2026 financial results: Strong execution and momentum continues; Raising 2026 operating earnings per share (EPS) guidance by 8% at the midpoint from our prior guidance. Net income was $126 million, or $1.33 per diluted share, and net operating income(1) was $120 million, or $1.26 per diluted share. Operating EPS grew 45% in the quarter and 39% year-to-date. Return on equity (ROE) of 10.9%; Operating ROE(5) of 13.1%, excluding significant items(5). Book value per share of $27.96 and book value per diluted share, excluding accumulated other comprehensive loss,(2) of $39.92, up 5%. Total new annualized premiums (NAP)(4) up 7%, extending our track record of insurance sales growth to 16 consecutive quarters. Achieved quarterly records in Worksite Division NAP, Annuity collected premiums and client assets in brokerage and advisory. Consumer and Worksite delivered their 14th and 16th consecutive quarters of producing agent count growth, respectively. "CNO delivered a very strong first half, with second quarter operating earnings per share up 45% and our 16th consecutive quarter of sales growth," said Gary C. Bhojwani, chief executive officer. "We are raising full-year guidance on operating earnings per share to reflect strong underlying fundamentals, continued profitability improvement and the consistent, repeatable results we continue to generate across the business." Net operating income, a non-GAAP(a) financial measure, excludes these non-economic accounting impacts as well as other non-operating items. Net operating income is used consistently by CNO's management to evaluate the operating performance of the Company and is a measure commonly used in the life insurance industry. It differs from net income primarily because it excludes the non-operating items as defined in note (1). Management believes an analysis of net operating income is important in understanding the profitability and operating trends of the Company's business. Net income is the most directly comparable GAAP measure. In 2Q26 and 2Q25, net income and net operating income(1) were unaffected by significant items. Significant items are detailed in note (6). Investment income not allocated to product lines includes investment income on investments in excess of amounts allocated to product lines, investments held by our holding companies, the spread we earn from our Federal Home Loan Bank ("FHLB") investment borrowing and FABN programs and variable components of investment income (including call and prepayment income, adjustments to returns on structured securities due to cash flow changes, income (loss) from company-owned life insurance ("COLI") and alternative investment income not allocated to product lines), net of interest expense on corporate debt and financing arrangements. The spread earned from our FHLB investment borrowing and FABN programs includes the investment income on the matched assets less: (i) interest on investment borrowings related to the FHLB investment borrowing program; (ii) interest credited on funding agreements; and (iii) amortization of deferred acquisition costs related to the FABN program. title: NEW JERSEY RESOURCES APPOINTS NEW CORPORATE SECRETARY
body_text: New Jersey Resources NEW JERSEY RESOURCES APPOINTS NEW CORPORATE SECRETARY 06/06/2022 - For Immediate Release Wall, N.J. — New Jersey Resources (NYSE: NJR) today announced the appointment of Tejal K. Mehta as Corporate Secretary and Assistant General Counsel effective June 6, 2022. In this role, Ms. Mehta will serve as the secretary to the board of directors of NJR and its subsidiaries, act as the company’s registered agent and keeper of records, provide oversight of the company’s corporate governance and support NJR’s overall corporate legal function. “Tejal Mehta is an accomplished lawyer whose proven skills and experience will serve our company, board and customers well,” said Richard Reich, senior vice president and general counsel of New Jersey Resources. “With nearly 15 years of legal experience and a proven record of effectively managing complex regulatory, corporate governance and oversight matters, we are pleased to welcome Tejal to our team.” Prior to joining NJR, Ms. Mehta served as Senior Counsel and Assistant Corporate Secretary at TD Bank Group, where she was responsible for regulatory compliance, corporate governance policy and corporate secretarial operations for TD's U.S. entities. Before that she was a Senior Associate in the White Collar Defense and Internal Investigations Group and the Securities Litigation Group at Ballard Spahr LLP, a nationally recognized corporate litigation firm. Ms. Mehta received her juris doctorate cum laude from Villanova School of Law and her bachelor of science degree from Widener University. She clerked for Magistrate Judge Carol Sandra Moore Wells in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, and is a member of the South Asian Bar Association of Philadelphia Board. About New Jersey Resources New Jersey Resources (NYSE: NJR) is a Fortune 1000 company that, through its subsidiaries, provides safe and reliable natural gas and clean energy services, including transportation, distribution, asset management and home services. NJR is composed of five primary businesses: New Jersey Natural Gas , NJR’s principal subsidiary, operates and maintains over 7,600 miles of natural gas transportation and distribution infrastructure to serve over half a million customers in New Jersey’s Monmouth, Ocean and parts of Morris, Middlesex and Burlington counties. Clean Energy Ventures invests in, owns and operates solar projects with a total capacity of nearly 370 megawatts, providing residential and commercial customers with low-carbon solutions. Energy Services manages a diversified portfolio of natural gas transportation and storage assets and provides physical natural gas services and customized energy solutions to its customers across North America. Storage and Transportation serves customers from local distributors and producers to electric generators and wholesale marketers through its ownership of Leaf River and the Adelphia Gateway Pipeline Project, as well as our 50% equity ownership in the Steckman Ridge natural gas storage facility. Home Services provides service contracts as well as heating, central air conditioning, water heaters, standby generators, solar and other indoor and outdoor comfort products to residential homes throughout New Jersey. NJR and its over 1,200 employees are committed to helping customers save energy and money by promoting conservation and encouraging efficiency through Conserve to Preserve® and initiatives such as The SAVEGREEN Project® and The Sunlight Advantage® . title: What Is HACCP? A Plain-English Guide for Operators
summary: HACCP is the food-safety system behind every clean inspection. Here's what it is, the 7 principles, and how multi-unit operators run it across every location.
body_text: Most operators meet HACCP the hard way: an inspector asks to see the plan, and someone starts digging through a binder nobody has opened since the last manager left. It doesn't have to be like that. HACCP in one sentence: HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) is a written food-safety system that finds the points in your process where food can become unsafe and puts specific controls in place to stop it. It's the logic behind almost every clean health inspection. HACCP isn't paperwork for its own sake. It's a way of thinking about your kitchen that keeps people from getting sick — written down so anyone on the line can follow it, and so you can prove it happened. It started in the 1960s as a collaboration between Pillsbury, NASA, and the U.S. Army to keep astronauts from getting food poisoning in space, and it's since become the framework the FDA builds retail food safety around. What does HACCP stand for? Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. Break it in half and it explains itself: Hazard Analysis — figure out what could make your food unsafe. Critical Control Points — find the specific steps where you can stop those hazards, and control them every time. Everything else in HACCP is the machinery that makes those two ideas repeatable across every shift and every store. What are the three types of hazards? Before you can control hazards, you have to know what you're looking for. HACCP groups them three ways: Biological — bacteria, viruses, parasites. Raw poultry, unwashed produce, a sick employee. This is where most foodborne illness comes from. Chemical — cleaning agents, sanitizer residue, allergens treated as a chemical hazard. Physical — anything that shouldn't be in the food: a metal shaving from a worn slicer, glass, a bit of packaging. Most of your day-to-day risk is biological, which is why so much of HACCP comes down to time and temperature. (If you want the foundation there, start with what counts as a TCS food and the temperature danger zone .) What are the 7 principles of HACCP? This is the heart of it. The FDA lays out seven principles , and they run in order — each one builds on the last. Here they are in kitchen terms. Principle What it actually means Kitchen example Conduct a hazard analysis Walk your menu and process; find where a hazard could get in Raw chicken cross-contaminating a prep surface Determine critical control points (CCPs) Find the steps where you can actually stop or reduce the hazard The cook step; the cooling step Establish critical limits Set the exact number that separates safe from unsafe Cook poultry to 165°F Establish monitoring Decide who checks, how, and how often Probe the thickest part of every chicken batch Establish corrective actions Decide what happens when a limit is missed — and record it Re-cook or discard; log what you did Establish verification Prove the system is working Calibrate thermometers; a manager reviews logs Establish recordkeeping Keep the documentation that proves all of the above Temperature logs, corrective action logs Want the wall version? Print this one and tape it inside the walk-in. Get the free one-page HACCP quick-reference card → If you only remember one thing about principle 7, make it this: if it isn't written down, as far as the health department is concerned, it didn't happen. A clean record of a problem you caught and fixed impresses an inspector more than a suspiciously perfect log. What's the difference between HACCP and a food safety plan? People use the terms loosely, but they aren't the same thing. HACCP is the specific, hazard-based system with the seven principles above. A broader food safety management system wraps HACCP together with your prerequisite programs — supplier controls, sanitation, personal hygiene, pest control. The FDA's model Food Code leans on the idea of "active managerial control," which is really just HACCP thinking applied to daily operations instead of living in a static document. The short version for a multi-unit operator: the seven principles are the engine; the prerequisite programs are the chassis. You need both. Do restaurants legally need a HACCP plan? It depends on what you do. A full, formal HACCP plan is federally required for specific operations — juice, seafood, and USDA-regulated meat and poultry processing. Most retail restaurants aren't required to hold one unless they do something a health department flags as specialized: reduced-oxygen packaging (sous vide, vacuum-sealing), curing, smoking for preservation, or acidifying rice for sushi. Those usually trigger a HACCP plan variance from your local authority. But here's the thing: whether it's legally mandatory or not, running your operation on HACCP logic is how you pass inspections and how you survive an outbreak investigation with your brand intact. The plan is the point, not the paperwork. How do you run HACCP across many locations? This is where it gets real for anyone responsible for more than one kitchen. A plan that lives in one good manager's head doesn't scale, and a plan that's different at every store is impossible to audit. Three things make it work across an estate: Standardize the process, not just the recipe. The critical limits and monitoring steps should be identical whether the store is in Toledo or Tucson. That's what lets a regional director compare stores honestly. Make monitoring hard to skip and easy to prove. Paper logs get "pencil-whipped" — filled in from memory at the end of a shift. A check that records itself in the moment removes both the temptation and the doubt. Give HQ a live view. The whole reason to run a system is that someone above store level can see when a limit gets blown and whether the corrective action actually happened. Without that, you have 40 binders and no visibility. This is the honest case for digital records over paper — not that digital is trendy, but that a temperature check logged on BOHA! Temp or a task confirmed on BOHA! Checklist becomes an audit-ready record HQ can actually see, instead of a clipboard in a drawer. Monitoring, corrective actions, and verification stop being three disconnected chores and become one record you can hand an inspector. The bottom line HACCP isn't exotic. It's hazard analysis, a handful of control points, the right limits, honest monitoring, and a record you can defend. The operators who sleep well are the ones who made those things automatic — at every location, not just the flagship. Next: if you're ready to actually build one, read How to Build a HACCP Plan for a Restaurant (publishing Aug 6) Frequently asked questions Is HACCP the same as ServSafe? No. ServSafe is a food-safety training and certification program from the National Restaurant Association. HACCP is the underlying system that training teaches you to run. What are the 7 principles of HACCP? Conduct a hazard analysis; determine critical control points; establish critical limits; establish monitoring; establish corrective actions; establish verification; and establish recordkeeping. How often should a HACCP plan be reviewed? At least annually, and any time you change a menu item, a process, a supplier, or equipment that affects a critical control point. Does a small or single-unit restaurant need HACCP? The principles apply at any size — a single kitchen can run the same seven-principle logic on a one-page plan. Whether a formal, written plan is legally required depends on your processes and your local health department.

title: Flowly Book Review: Back Mechanic by Stuart McGill
body_text: We are excited to bring you another thrilling book review as part of our Flowly Book Review Series! This week, we invite you to join us on an exploration of Back Mechanic as Christine, a valued member of the Flowly team, takes us on a journey through its pages. The views expressed in this blog are solely those of the reviewer and do not necessarily reflect the opinions or position of Flowly. Why did you choose to read Back Mechanic ? Like everyone in the United States, I've been following the news regarding Brian Thompson, United Healthcare CEO, and Luigi Mangione since our team first heard the news. When we heard about Luigi's experience with chronic back pain and discovered that he read and reviewed some books about back pain, we immediately decided to read them to see if there was any applicable advice we could pass on to our heroes. I picked Back Mechanic to read first because Luigi's review stated that this book was more useful than Crooked . What’s it about? In a world filled with countless back products promising quick fixes, a comprehensive guide to self-assessment and recovery is crucial. Back Mechanic offers a step-by-step approach to identifying the causes of your pain and provides strategies to avoid setbacks in your recovery journey. The book features a progressive exercise program designed to strengthen and rehabilitate your back. Developed by spine specialist Prof. McGill, this guide is built on over 30 years of research and clinical expertise. Through this evidence-based resource, you’ll gain the tools to take control of your back health and become your own advocate. Richly illustrated, Back Mechanic empowers you to rebuild your life. What are the main takeaways? While this book is a great starting point for those with back pain on maintaining healthy physical back health, a lot of Dr. Stuart Mcgill's understanding of nonstructural back pain is severely outdated. A lot has changed since he first penned this book in 2015, and I'm disappointed that there isn't an updated version to reflect these changes. However, I thought it was really interesting that our philosophy at Flowly and his intention to write his book are similar. We also don't think that people with chronic pain should go through surgery or be prescribed heavy pain medication to be able to live their lives pain-free. We also know and agree with him that the healing journey won't happen overnight, nor will it be easy for the patients. It's a lifelong journey. And, like Dr. McGill, we at Flowly try to give our heroes all the tools they need to have better days than bad. - Outdated Info #1: Dr Stuart McGill believes that there is no such thing as nonstructural pain (aka nonspecific or psychosomatic pain). He believes that all back pain has a cause that can be addressed. The self-assessment he provides is geared towards pinpointing structural pain and would not apply to our heroes with nonstructural pain whose pain is asymmetrical, varies in intensity throughout the day, migrates to different locations, etc. If we had our heroes go through this self-assessment, many would not be able to pinpoint their cause because it would not apply to their situation. His opinion on talk therapy is that it doesn't do much for pain. We agree. Traditional talk therapy was not meant to help people with their chronic pain. Since 2015, there have been significant advances, and we now have pain-informed therapies like pain-reprocessing therapy (PRT) and emotional awareness and expression therapy (EAET). This new pain-informed therapy goes beyond what Dr. McGill considers to be psychotherapy as the focus is on addressing the root of the pain and not on the "Psychosocial issues, such as whether or not an individual likes their job, or whether or not a patient is neurotic." - Outdated Info #2: Dr Stuart Mcgill's opinion on alternative modalities for back pain treatment (physical therapy and Pilates) is based primarily on his experience prior to publishing this book in 2015. For example, he considers physical therapy as a "passive treatment" where something is being done to you vs. an "active treatment" that requires the patient to participate in some manner that works towards the cure. Since writing his book in 2015, there have been significant strides and innovations in the physical and occupational therapy vocations. I would argue that most PT/OT are now more active, where patients are relearning how to move and use their bodies correctly instead of getting the treatment done to them. I can see this on social media where PT-content creators share exercises with their followers vs. showing passive treatments to sell through their services. At Flowly, we're partnering with physical therapy clinics so that we're approaching pain from both sides, where our heroes not only shift their relationship with pain but also learn how to move in a way that doesn't cause physical stress and inflammation to their bodies. Additionally, as someone entering her fifth year of doing Pilates consistently, it's clear that Dr Mcgill's expertise in Pilates is limited to what he's been exposed to in 2015. When he's talking about how pilates encourages "flattening of the neutral spine," which can amplify back pain, he's mainly referencing classical pilates. Contemporary pilates emphasizes maintaining the neutral spine much more and incorporates elements from physical therapy, yoga, etc. - Outdated Info #3 (and the biggest, in my opinion): The medical landscape has changed significantly since he wrote this handbook. We see now that there are more working in the healthcare industry who also believe that surgery or opioids are not the best - or only - answers to chronic pain. There's an overwhelming number of new research that I hope he includes if he ever writes an updated version. How did Back Mechanic affect you? I think it's reaffirmed my belief that I need to continue to maintain healthy physical habits so that I can continue to have a healthy back and spine as I get older. While I believe the book is outdated in context, his content (e.g., his plan) is timeless and applies to anyone wanting to learn how to maintain good spine/back health. I will be incorporating some of his guidelines and strategies into my life. (For those who want to know what they are, the top two I'll be implementing are daily brisk walking to help unload the pressure on my spine and improving my posture during my daily activities). Who should read Back Mechanic ? Anyone who has structural back issues and wants a clearly written, thoughtful guide on improving their physical back health should read this book. While not everyone in our community has chronic back pain, the plan he outlines is a great starting point for our heroes who want to slowly incorporate more movement into their lives. It's a great plan for them to work on improving their back health since our core is so essential to our everyday activities. Additionally, if any of our heroes are considering if they need movement therapy, the self-assessment in this book is a great starting point for evaluation. However, I would like to stress the importance of remembering the time period in which this book was written and coming to your own conclusions about the other modalities he mentions in this book, as they may no longer be applicable to you, your situation, or in general. What real‑world results can you expect? Companies that move to AI-driven dunning typically lift recovery rates by 12%–18% and cut 3–5 days off the cash-to-cash cycle. That turns a churn source into a retention play. In one proof-of-concept using Random Forest risk models, a firm dropped late-payment volume from 42.5% to 28% of invoices and freed up enough cash flow to fund a new product line inside a quarter. A pure rule-based setup still beat manual chasing by 30% on speed, but barely moved churn. The messages felt generic, and customers could tell. Our recommendation: If you process more than 200 invoices a month and already track subscription health, buy the AI-enhanced tool. Below that threshold, or without any data-science help on the team, start rule-based and upgrade later. Skipping automation entirely only makes sense when manual chasing already runs under an hour a week and your missed-payment rate stays below 5%. Everything else is choosing where you want to sit on the speed-versus-experience line as you grow. Why Dunning and Collections Automation Matters Modern subscription tracking software with dunning and collections automation lets you chase a missed payment the moment it happens, turning a cash-flow hole into a recovery loop. The catch is tone. Pair speed with the wrong voice and you trade fast cash for a canceled account. Blixo’s SaaS service runs a full-stack dunning workflow built to recover failed transactions while holding down involuntary churn. Smart-retry logic sits on top of automated notifications, so when a card expires or a charge fails, the system can try alternative payment methods on its own. Agents stop hand-writing notices and reconciling payments, and get their time back for work that actually needs a human. How does automation balance speed with customer experience? The dunning journey splits into three phases, each with a job. Invisible smart retries run in the background the second a charge fails, testing alternative payment methods without bothering the customer. Gentle nudges follow: personalized, low-friction messages that remind users what they’d lose access to. Escalation kicks in only when the account is high-value or the failure sticks, handing off to a person who can negotiate a payment plan. “Dunning is not a collections function. It’s a customer‑success function with billing infrastructure underneath.” – Baremetrics Keep the first two phases automated and you get the speed. Save the human touch for last and you keep the trust. That’s the same pattern the better platforms hit with AI-driven smart retries that resolve issues quietly, then shift to a customer-first tone when a message is actually needed. When is full automation the wrong choice? Skip end-to-end automation for businesses running highly customized enterprise contracts with bespoke payment terms. Rigid automated rules can trample a high-touch relationship, and a manual, personal approach earns more back. Same logic if your price point is very high and each account is effectively a partnership. Human-first outreach from day one beats looking like a robot came to collect. What tangible savings can you expect? Agent time: Early-stage automation kills the manual notice-writing, so teams can spend that time on upsells and support. Revenue lift: Consistent decline management catches late payments before cards expire, which pulls more revenue into recognition. Cash-flow health: Faster recoveries shrink days-sales-outstanding and steady the cash position. For more on how structured dunning feeds retention, see our guide on What is Dunning, and Can it Improve Customer Retention? Core Elements of a Dunning Workflow A dunning workflow really has three linked parts: automated payment retries, intelligent decline handling, and customer-centric communication. Embed those in subscription tracking software with dunning and collections automation and you can chase a missed invoice the instant it happens while keeping the tone that holds the relationship together. Get the mix of speed and empathy right and you recover revenue without inflating churn. In practice, the transition logic between stages is where most of the work lives. The system watches payment status in real time and reads each account’s risk profile before it moves anything from background processing to active outreach. Set clear rules for when an account crosses that line, and customers only hear from you after the automated attempts are genuinely spent. How do we structure payment retries for speed without hurting experience? Start with automated retries that respect card-issuer rules and time attempts to real processing windows. Blixo’s collections engine schedules retries to avoid the pointless failures that burn through issuer goodwill. Add customizable dunning settings and you can decide how aggressively retries run for each risk level, so most customers never notice a thing. What communication strategy keeps customers happy while we chase payments? A multi-channel, tone-adjusted cadence that starts before the payment actually fails. Pre-dunning alerts (“your card expires soon”) give customers a chance to fix the problem with zero negative language. If a charge does fail, a structured email sequence follows, backed by SMS, in-app notices, or letters for mobile-first users. Every message leads with the value they still get, not the debt they owe. Blixo’s reminder system lets you pick the channels your audience actually reads, and you can layer in phone calls for accounts where a personal touch pays off. When should we pause or escalate service without losing trust? Escalation only fires after the first two phases run dry. Your own rules set the thresholds: pause access, downgrade the plan, or route to a customer-experience specialist. For premium clients, a short pause plus a dedicated outreach call can flip a would-be cancel into a stronger relationship. For smaller accounts, pause billing but keep the product live so they can reactivate whenever they’re ready. Speed first, experience close behind. Stitch automated retries, rule-based decline handling, and empathetic multi-channel messaging together and you land the sweet spot: cash comes back fast and the customer still feels respected. That balance is what separates a dunning tool that scales from one that quietly bleeds accounts. Automating Collections: From Retry to Revenue Recovery A subscription tracking software with dunning and collections automation can turn a missed charge into a quick win without alienating anyone. When a payment fails, Blixo coordinates background recovery with the customer-facing touchpoints, so you recover cash fast and the relationship stays intact. Configuring Payment Retries in Blixo Blixo lets you build retry schedules that follow issuer guidelines and respect your timing. You control how many attempts, how far apart, and what happens when retries run out. Retry schedule : Set how many times and how often the system attempts the charge after a failure. Maximum attempts : Cap the retries so you never loop endlessly, and auto-advance the account to the next phase when you hit the limit. Audit trail : Every attempt is logged, giving finance a clean record with no manual entry. “Dunning is about politely reminding customers about overdue payments, focusing on retaining customers while recouping lost revenue.” – Stripe Multi‑Channel Strategies for Revenue Recovery Blixo’s collections feature reaches customers on the channels they actually respond to, without dropping the courteous tone. Email reminders : A sequence that opens friendly and gets more direct over time. SMS nudges : Short texts with a one-click payment link for fast action. Phone calls and letters : Optional voice or mail for accounts that warrant a personal touch. Content and timing are yours to set on each channel, so the outreach reads as helpful, not pushy. When to Use Segmentation for Collections Once failed payments outgrow what a person can chase by hand, Blixo’s settings let you segment accounts on criteria you define, like invoice size or customer type. Send your higher-value accounts down a more intensive follow-up path and let automation handle the rest. Custom segmentation : Group accounts by plan tier or outstanding amount and apply different reminder schedules. Prioritized workflow : Route higher-risk or higher-value accounts to a hands-on escalation path while the engine handles the routine cases. Configurable retries, multi-channel nudges, and optional segmentation together get you the balance you’re after: fast recovery, positive experience. That’s what lifts recovery rates while keeping the trust that funds long-term growth. Integrating Dunning with Payment Gateways and Billing Systems A subscription tracking software with dunning and collections automation only gets fast when it talks straight to the payment gateway and the billing ledger. In Blixo, a declined card triggers an automated retry, updates the account status, and fires a personalized reminder. No manual handoff anywhere in that loop. The integration layer is the fulcrum of the whole speed-versus-experience trade-off. A clean API bridge removes the lag between a failed charge and the next smart retry, and it keeps every notification’s tone matched to the latest payment-method data. When gateway and billing stay in sync, you dodge the “payment-not-found” errors that frustrate users and push them out the door. How Do We Connect Dunning Logic to Payment Gateways? Through webhook listeners and idempotent retry endpoints. The gateway posts a payment_failed event to a secure URL; the dunning engine records it, runs the smart-retry schedule, and calls the gateway’s retry endpoint with the original transaction ID. Because the call is idempotent, repeat attempts never double-charge the card. Double-charging is the fastest way to lose the trust you’re trying to protect. Webhook security : verify signatures and enforce TLS so no one can spoof a failure. Retry payload : include transaction_id , amount , and a retry_reason flag so the gateway can apply issuer-specific rules. Response handling : read success, temporary decline, or permanent failure codes to decide between a nudge and an escalation. Keep the integration responsive and you fix cash-flow timing without burying the customer in redundant emails. What Data Mapping Practices Keep the Customer Experience Intact? We map three core objects between the billing system and the dunning workflow: customer profile, payment method, and invoice status. A stable customer_id is the primary key, and every gateway event carries it so the billing record updates instantly. When an Account Updater service flags an expired card, Blixo can refresh the stored payment token before the next retry, so the customer never feels the friction. Field alignment : standardize last4 , expiry_month , and expiry_year across systems so nothing mismatches. State machine : define clear states ( pending , retrying , awaiting_customer , canceled ) with transition rules that trigger the right channel. Audit trail : log every sync event with timestamps. That log becomes the source of truth for support and cuts manual investigation time. When the data stays consistent, your messages can name the exact problem (“your card ending in 1234 expired”) and the tone reads helpful instead of accusatory. In the U.S., a large share of invoices land after the due date, and the U.K. shows the same pattern, with billions in unpaid debt behind it. Feed real-time decline signals into an automated dunning loop and the gains show up fast: a SaaS consultancy cut its days-sales-outstanding, and a digital media publisher recovered more revenue without any bump in churn. “A seamless integration ensures that the billing system and the payment gateway act as a single source of truth, preventing embarrassing double-billing errors.” Machine-learning risk scores sharpen the call on who gets a gentle reminder versus a direct phone call, letting high-value accounts stay in the smart-retry phase longer. Cash lands faster, often the same business day, and the customer still feels respected. Build those connections well and you scale without spending down customer goodwill. Choosing the Right Dunning Automation Platform When you evaluate subscription tracking software with dunning and collections automation , the first question is whether it can turn a missed charge into cash in minutes and still sound friendly. Speed only pays when the messaging respects the customer’s context. Otherwise the speed advantage just becomes faster churn. Think of the trade-off as a two-axis matrix, and plot your business on it to see where the current process leaks revenue. Recover fast but generate a wall of complaints, and you’re sitting in the high-speed, low-impact quadrant. The goal is both axes at once: outreach smart enough to keep goodwill while it accelerates collection. What core features should we prioritize? The capabilities that move you toward that quadrant: Pre-dunning management – step in before a subscription enters the formal dunning flow, cutting involuntary churn. Smart-retry logic – follow issuer-recommended intervals and skip the pointless retries that irritate customers. Multi-channel, behavior-driven notifications (email, SMS, in-app) – match tone to the customer’s recent activity. Real-time collector dashboard – surface overdue accounts instantly so agents step in only when automation stalls. Advanced segmentation – group accounts by risk or payment history so you can choose a gentle nudge versus a firmer reminder. How do we evaluate pricing without sacrificing speed? Treat pricing as cost-per-recovery, not a flat subscription fee. Take the average value of a recovered invoice and compare it to the platform’s per-transaction charge. If the platform costs $0.25 per recovered dollar and you recover $0.40 on average, the net gain covers the expense. Walk away from solutions charging high flat fees for low volume; the overhead eats the speed benefit. Look for usage-based tiers that unlock the advanced features, like segmentation, only when your volume justifies them. That keeps you from paying for tools you don’t touch yet, while leaving room to scale automation as growth demands. What implementation steps keep the balance intact? Sandbox trial – mirror one high-risk segment and measure days-to-cash against the customer-impact score, side by side. Pre-dunning alerts – set triggers (say, 48 hours before a card expires) to head off late payments. Smart-retry schedule – respect issuer rules so you don’t waste attempts. Multi-channel notification flow – start with a polite email, escalate to SMS only after two unanswered attempts. Collector dashboard integration – wire the dashboard to your CRM so any manual outreach inherits the automation’s context and the handoff stays clean. For the first month, track recovery rates against benchmarks (roughly one in four is a common target). If you fall short, adjust the segmentation thresholds and cadence. That iterative loop lets you scale speed while you keep polishing the experience. Align features, pricing, and rollout around the speed-experience matrix and dunning automation stops being a chore. It becomes a trust-building engine that funds sustainable growth. Implementing Dunning and Collections Automation with Blixo Blixo’s dunning and collections automation turns a missed charge into a cash-in event while keeping the communication clear and courteous. Automate the reminders and follow-ups, and you cut manual effort while raising the odds of getting paid on time. What core features support fast and friendly collections? Automated reminders – Schedule email, SMS, phone, or letter reminders that fire automatically once a payment goes overdue. Custom dunning steps – Build a sequence that moves from friendly to firmer, in your brand’s voice. Task management & aging reports – See outstanding invoices in an aging dashboard and assign collection tasks so nothing slips. These keep the approach professional and human while cash flow speeds up. How to configure the dunning workflow in Blixo Set up a reminder schedule – Pick how many attempts and the intervals between them (2 days, 5 days, 10 days). Blixo sends the chosen channel at each step. Tailoring automation to your business needs Adjust reminder frequency – For high-value accounts, use fewer reminders on longer intervals; for riskier accounts, add extra steps. Customize message content – Bring your own wording, branding, and product details into each template so the tone matches the rest of the customer experience. Line the dunning workflow up with your own processes and Blixo collects efficiently while keeping the relationship intact. Frequently Asked Questions 1. How can I determine whether AI‑driven dunning is worth the pilot investment for a business processing 120 invoices per month? AI‑driven dunning becomes cost‑effective when the projected incremental recovery exceeds the pilot expense within three to six months. For 120 invoices monthly, a typical pilot costs $2,000 and can boost recovery by 10‑12 %, translating to $1,500‑$2,000 extra cash, reaching break‑even by month four. 2. What steps should I take if a payment gateway stops sending webhook events during the dunning cycle? First verify that the webhook endpoint is reachable and the secret signature matches. If the gateway’s health page shows outages, enable a temporary polling loop that queries recent events via the API. Once events resume, replay any missed failures manually through the dunning console to keep the flow intact. 3. Can I mix rule‑based retries with AI risk scoring in the same workflow, and how does that affect maintenance effort? Blixo’s hybrid flow merges deterministic rules with AI risk scores, letting low‑risk accounts follow a simple retry cadence while high‑risk ones receive probability‑based timing. Maintenance rises modestly to about three hours per month, because while the AI component adapts automatically, the underlying rule engine still benefits from periodic manual adjustments to align with changing business policies. 4. How does dunning automation handle customers with regulatory constraints, such as GDPR or PCI DSS requirements? Compliance is built into the dunning pipeline by encrypting all payment tokens and never storing raw card numbers, satisfying PCI DSS. Personal data used for notifications is pseudonymized, and any EU‑resident information must be retained in a GDPR‑approved region. Audits should run quarterly to confirm adherence. 5. What are common misconceptions about pausing service access during dunning, and when is it advisable to avoid it? Pausing service access is often assumed to pressure payment, but it can trigger churn for users who rely on continuous availability. It is advisable to keep the product active and only restrict premium features until the invoice clears, especially for SaaS products where downtime directly reduces perceived value. 6. How do I measure the “customer‑impact score” without a built‑in metric from the platform? To approximate a customer‑impact score without native analytics, track the response rate to each reminder channel, correlate those rates with subsequent churn, and assign weighted points (e.g., email = 1, SMS = 2). Summing points per account yields a relative impact metric that can be benchmarked against industry averages. 7. If my subscription plans include multiple currencies, does the automation adjust retry timing based on local banking holidays? Automation platforms that support multi‑currency can reference a calendar of banking holidays per locale and postpone retries until the next business day. If the system lacks this feature, you must import holiday tables manually and adjust the retry schedule via custom rules, ensuring that attempts are not blocked by regional closures.
